title: Lecture 1: What is Computation?
notes: Declarative knowledge ('what is true') vs Imperative knowledge ('how-to recipe').
Fixed-program computers vs Stored-program computers (von Neumann architecture).
Python data types: int, float, bool, NoneType, and basic scalar expressions.

transcript.text: Welcome to 6.0001, Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python. I am John Guttag.
Computer science is not really about computers, any more than physics is about particle accelerators.
Declarative knowledge states facts. Imperative knowledge provides recipes: how to compute.
In Python, everything is an object with a type and attributes.

title: Lecture 2: Branching and Iteration
notes: Branching programs with if, elif, else.
Looping with while and for loops.
Loop invariants and guaranteed termination using decreasing counter variables.

transcript.text: Today we add control flow: branching and iteration to make programs execute selectively.
Indentation in Python defines block structure and lexical scope.
Every loop must possess a decrementing function that proves termination.

title: Lecture 3: String Manipulation, Guess and Check, Approximations, Bisection
notes: Strings as immutable sequences: indexing and slicing s[start:stop:step].
Exhaustive enumeration (guess-and-check).
Approximation algorithms with epsilon tolerance.
Bisection search: exponential speedup cutting search space in half each step.

transcript.text: In Lecture 3, Dr. Ana Bell covers string manipulations and bisection search.
Exhaustive enumeration checks every candidate. Bisection search uses monotonicity to eliminate half the remaining space.
Bisection search converges in logarithmic O(log N) iterations.

title: Lecture 4: Decomposition, Abstraction, and Functions
notes: Decomposition: structuring monolithic code into self-contained modules.
Abstraction: treating a function as a black-box contract via docstrings and signatures.
Variable scope: local stack frames and lexical scoping.

transcript.text: Functions suppress implementation details so we can architect complex software systems.
Formal parameters receive arguments passed by assignment.
Variables initialized inside a function exist strictly within its local frame stack.

title: Lecture 5: Tuples, Lists, Aliasing, Mutability, and Cloning
notes: Tuples: immutable ordered sequences of elements.
Lists: mutable sequences with append, extend, and in-place mutation.
Aliasing vs cloning: modifying an aliased list changes all referenced variables.

transcript.text: Lecture 5 explores compound data types: tuples and mutable lists.
Tuples are immutable; lists are mutable objects whose internal elements can change in memory.
Aliasing occurs when two variable names point to the exact same memory address.

title: Lecture 6: Recursion and Dictionaries
notes: Inductive step and base cases in recursive functions.
Towers of Hanoi and Fibonacci via recursion.
Dictionaries: key-value hash maps with O(1) expected lookup and insertion.

transcript.text: Today we study recursion and Python dictionaries.
A recursive function calls itself on smaller instances until reaching a base case.
Dictionaries map hashable keys to arbitrary values with near-instantaneous O(1) lookup.

title: Lecture 7: Testing, Debugging, Exceptions, and Assertions
notes: Unit testing and regression testing.
Handling runtime errors gracefully using try, except, raise, and finally blocks.
Assertions as defensive preconditions.

transcript.text: Every programmer writes bugs. Today we discuss systematic testing, debugging, and exceptions.
Defensive programming validates assumptions early before silent corruption occurs.
Try-except blocks intercept exceptions and enable predictable error recovery.

title: Lecture 8: Object Oriented Programming
notes: Abstract Data Types (ADTs) bundle state and operations together.
Defining classes: the __init__ constructor and self parameter.
Special dunder methods: __str__, __add__, __len__.

transcript.text: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) allows us to create our own custom data types.
A class is a blueprint; an instance is a concrete realization in memory.
Methods are functions bound to instances, receiving self as their first argument.

title: Lecture 9: Python Classes and Inheritance
notes: Subclasses inherit attributes and methods from superclasses.
Method overriding and extending functionality via super().
Polymorphism and class hierarchies in software architecture.

transcript.text: In Lecture 9, we examine class inheritance and polymorphism.
Inheritance enables code reuse: sub-types inherit attributes from base classes.
Overriding allows derived classes to customize behavior while honoring the parent interface.

title: Lecture 10: Understanding Program Efficiency, Part 1
notes: Measuring program efficiency: wall-clock time vs counting primitive operations.
Asymptotic analysis: Big O notation O(f(n)).
Common complexity classes: constant O(1), logarithmic O(log n), linear O(n), polynomial O(n^c), exponential O(2^n).

transcript.text: How do we reason about whether an algorithm will scale to big datasets? Big O notation.
Big O provides an asymptotic upper bound as input size n approaches infinity.
We ignore multiplicative constants and lower-order terms to classify the dominant growth rate.

title: Lecture 11: Understanding Program Efficiency, Part 2
notes: Analyzing iterative and recursive algorithms.
Exponential complexity of power set generation and recursive Fibonacci.
Trade-offs between time complexity and space complexity.

transcript.text: Lecture 11 dives deeper into asymptotic analysis, particularly for recursive algorithms.
When each call branches into two recursive subproblems, depth d leads to 2^d operations.
Analyzing the recursive tree allows us to calculate total operations across all call frames.

title: Lecture 12: Searching and Sorting
notes: Linear search vs binary search on sorted sequences.
Bogo sort, Bubble sort, Selection sort, and Merge sort.
Divide-and-conquer merge sort achieving O(n log n) efficiency.

transcript.text: We conclude 6.0001 with search and sort algorithms.
Binary search finds an item in sorted list in logarithmic time.
Merge sort divides the list, sorts recursively, and merges sorted sublists in linear time.
